cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica); Bulang Shan population, including the local 'bitter' (ku cha) and 'sweet' (tian cha) strains
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried maocha, steamed and pressed into cakes or bricks. Bulang leaf is thick and tough, so it is often rolled harder than Yiwu leaf; some village processing leaves a faint smoky note from wood-fired woks.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the serious lots; autumn tea is softer and cheaper; a great deal of summer plantation leaf from the mountain goes into factory blends and shu.
appearance_dry: Dark, thick, tightly twisted leaves with silver-grey buds and sturdy stems, usually pressed into a dense cake.
appearance_liquor: Deep gold to orange when young, often slightly hazy in the first steeps, clear amber with a few years.
appearance_wet: Thick, broad olive-green leaves that stay leathery even after a long session.
taste_profile: Big bitterness and some astringency up front, a dense body, honey and tobacco-like depth underneath and a slow, strong returning sweetness; some lots carry a wisp of smoke.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Flash steeps for the first four or five infusions; this tea punishes long early steeps with bitterness. Clay pots round it off slightly, which some people like and some think is a waste.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and village, mostly as 357 g cakes, with a wide price spread between old-tree single-village tea and the mountain's large plantation output. Young Bulang (1–3 years) is bracing and bitter; it is the classic candidate for ageing, with the mid-aged window (roughly 7–15 years) turning the bitterness into dense sweetness, and the 1990s to early-2000s Menghai factory cakes, generally said to lean heavily on Bulang-area leaf, are the reference for what it becomes. Most of what is on sale today is 2005–2025; dry-stored cakes stay sharper for longer, while Guangdong-stored ones soften noticeably within five or six years.
description:
Bulang Shan is the big, bitter heart of Menghai County, a mountain township running down to the Myanmar border and named after the Bulang people who farm it. The Bulang are usually described as descendants of the ancient Pu peoples who cultivated tea here long before anyone pressed a cake, and the villages on these slopes (Lao Ban Zhang, Xin Ban Zhang, Lao Man E, Ban Pen, Man Xin Long, Mannuo) supply the strongest raw material in pu-erh.

The leaf is thick and oily, grown between roughly 1,200 and 1,900 m, and processed the standard sheng way: wok-fired, rolled, dried in the sun and pressed. Rolling tends to be firm, and old-fashioned wood-fired kill-green can leave a touch of smoke in the maocha that fades within a couple of years. The mountain also carries huge plantation areas, and much of that leaf goes to the Menghai factories for blends and for ripe tea.

In the cup, young Bulang is intense: real bitterness, a chewy body, honey and something like pipe tobacco underneath, and a returning sweetness that takes its time but then stays. Lao Man E, with its separate 'bitter' and 'sweet' tea strains, is the extreme of the style. It is the easiest sheng to over-brew, so keep the early infusions to a few seconds and judge it on steeps five to ten, when the bitterness has stepped back and the depth shows.

Buy it with the village and the year clearly stated. Because 'Bulang' is a township rather than one hillside, the word covers everything from gushu that rivals Lao Ban Zhang to cheap bush tea, and the gap in price between them is honest only when the material is. A thin, harsh, drying tea that never turns sweet is plantation leaf, whatever the wrapper says.

It is a big part of what aged into the classic 'Menghai flavour' of the famous old factory cakes, so if you are going to buy one cake to forget about in a cupboard for ten years, this is a sensible one.
